headline: Thermal drones help Kenya protect elephants and farmers
meta_description: Thermal drones are reducing human-elephant conflict in Kenya's Amboseli National Park, safely guiding nearly 2,000 elephants away from farms.
summary_short: In Kenya's Amboseli Park, thermal drones equipped with night-vision technology are successfully preventing dangerous encounters between elephants and farmers.
body:
Amboseli National Park's nearly 2,000 African elephants spend about 80% of their time outside the park's boundaries, wandering across farms and community lands in southern Kenya. For smallholder farmers like Dominic Mutua from Inkoisuk village, this meant staying up most nights to guard crops from hungry intruders. Now, conservation teams are using thermal drones to transform this age-old conflict into manageable coexistence. The drones, equipped with infrared sensors, track elephant movements in real time and guide herds away from farms with the sound of their propellers—which farmers describe as sounding like a swarm of bees. In just two months in 2026, these aerial sentries responded to 78 elephant incidents around the park, successfully redirecting elephants back into protected areas in 33 cases alone.

The technology addresses a persistent crisis: over a decade, the larger Amboseli region reported more than 9,000 human-wildlife conflict cases, with nearly half involving elephants. Retaliatory killings and injuries were common when farming families lost their livelihoods to crop raiding. Jeremy Goss, Program Director at Big Life Foundation, confirms the shift: "Thanks to the use of drones in wildlife conservation, we have seen a reduction in retaliatory injuries and deaths." The drones work alongside existing methods—fencing, ranger patrols, chili oil—but offer something those cannot: precision monitoring across Amboseli's ideal open plains and sparse tree cover, plus the ability to operate at night when elephants typically raid farms.

What makes this solution remarkable is its efficiency. The approximately 200,000 people living within and around the park's 8,093-square-kilometer region depend on overlapping lands with wildlife. Amboseli's survival hinges on community support. By preventing crop losses, the drones help communities view elephant conservation not as a threat to their survival, but as a shared responsibility—a quiet revolution in how humans and wildlife can coexist.
quick_facts: Nearly 2,000 elephants inhabit Amboseli National Park in Kenya
In 2 months, drones responded to 78 incidents, successfully redirecting 33 herds
Thermal drones use infrared sensors to track elephants at night
Over 9,000 human-wildlife conflicts reported in broader region over 10 years
Elephants spend 80% of time outside park boundaries on farmland
